topic-2-1-1.title: One bit string, different interpretations
topic-2-1-1.caption: An encoding supplies meaning. The bits alone do not tell a machine whether to treat \(01000001\) as a number or a character.

topic-2-1-2.title: AND as a complete input–output specification
topic-2-1-2.caption: The truth table lists four possible inputs. Only the input \(11\) produces one; a circuit must implement all four rows.

topic-2-1-3.title: OR written as a polynomial over bits
topic-2-1-3.caption: All additions are modulo two. The polynomial \(x+y+xy\) reproduces OR on Boolean inputs; its interpretation depends on this arithmetic.

topic-2-2-3.title: Three different inputs merge
topic-2-2-3.caption: The AND gate maps \(00\), \(01\), and \(10\) to the same output. Output zero cannot identify which of these inputs occurred.

topic-2-3-1.title: Resetting an unknown bit
topic-2-3-1.caption: Both possible logical inputs are reset to zero. For erasure of one equally likely bit in the standard isothermal setting, the minimum heat delivered to the environment is kBT ln 2.

topic-2-3-2.title: Logical and physical questions are separate
topic-2-3-2.caption: A reversible truth table settles whether the input is recoverable. It does not specify the energy dissipated by a particular physical device.

topic-2-3-3.title: Preserve the input; update the target
topic-2-3-3.caption: Configurations are written \(xt\), here with \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(1)=1\). \(U_f\) flips the target exactly when \(f(x)=1\), and applying it twice returns every configuration.

topic-2-4-1.title: A controlled operation has two branches
topic-2-4-1.caption: CNOT keeps the control, the first bit, and flips the target when the control is \(1\): \(10\) and \(11\) exchange. Exactly one arrow enters each configuration, so the step can be undone.

topic-4-1-1.title: Ket notation and coordinates
topic-4-1-1.caption: The two coordinates are ordered by the selected basis. The coefficients belong to basis vectors, not to two simultaneous measurement outcomes.

topic-4-2-1.title: Unitary evolution preserves state geometry
topic-4-2-1.caption: Every arrow ends on the unit circle: both states have length one before and after the operation. The same rotation carries \(\ket\psi\) to \(U\ket\psi\) and \(\ket\chi\) to \(U\ket\chi\), preserving the angle between them. This real-amplitude example shows a rotation in state space; general unitaries preserve inner products in complex state space.

topic-6-1-1.title: Independent preparation on two wires
topic-6-1-1.caption: A and B are single-qubit preparation unitaries. Their independent actions give the four joint amplitudes ac, ad, bc, bd; each box can require several elementary gates.

topic-6-1-3.title: A joint register and its readout
topic-6-1-3.caption: A joint unitary updates four amplitudes on two qubits, but measurement returns a single pair of bits. U denotes the complete operation, not a free elementary gate.

topic-6-2-2.title: A gate that prevents factorization
topic-6-2-2.caption: Before CNOT the two wires have a product state. After it, the coefficients of 00 and 11 are nonzero while those of 01 and 10 vanish; no product of two local vectors has these coefficients.

topic-6-2-3.title: Choose the readout circuit
topic-6-2-3.caption: The upper circuit measures a Bell pair directly. The lower circuit first applies H on both wires. Both give matching bits; the corresponding classical mixture gives all four pairs in the lower circuit.

topic-6-3-1.title: Copying basis labels
topic-6-3-1.caption: CNOT copies a basis label into a blank target. For a superposition the joint output is entangled, rather than two independent copies.

topic-6-3-2.title: The proposed copying circuit
topic-6-3-2.caption: U? is a hypothetical universal copying unitary, not an available gate. The required output overlap differs from the input overlap, so the two requested actions cannot belong to one unitary.

topic-6-3-3.title: Local operations and remote readout
topic-6-3-3.caption: H and CNOT prepare the shared Bell pair. Alice’s local gate UA cannot affect Bob’s outcome probabilities, even when Bob chooses a different readout gate V.

notes: Alice’s result is not sent to Bob.

topic-7-1-1.title: Four possible one-bit oracles
topic-7-1-1.caption: The four reversible circuits encode the four Boolean functions. They retain x and update y by XOR with f(x). This anticipates the reversible query definition in 7.1.3.

topic-7-1-2.title: Two classical value queries
topic-7-1-2.caption: Two separate basis-input runs of the reversible oracle reproduce classical value-query access. Each target is measured to read a function value; no superposition is used.

topic-7-1-3.title: The reversible query gate
topic-7-1-3.caption: The box acts on both wires and retains the input label. One use counts as one query in the specified oracle model.

topic-7-2-1.title: Evaluate on a superposition
topic-7-2-1.caption: H prepares both input alternatives coherently. The oracle acts on their joint superposition; it has not supplied two classical answers.

topic-7-2-2.title: Read one input–value pair
topic-7-2-2.caption: Both wires are measured after one query. A run returns either (0,f(0)) or (1,f(1)), each with probability one half.

topic-7-2-3.title: A workspace record changes interference
topic-7-2-3.caption: The target starts at zero and can retain the input branch. For a balanced function, the final H on the input cannot make its outcome definite.

notes: A target record prevents cancellation when f is balanced.

topic-7-3-1.title: Flip eigenstates on a wire
topic-7-3-1.caption: X leaves the plus state unchanged and multiplies the minus state by a common minus sign. In a controlled operation that factor becomes a relative phase between control alternatives.

topic-7-3-3.title: Compute, phase, uncompute
topic-7-3-3.caption: A computes the answer and workspace. Z changes the answer-one sign. The inverse A restores the answer and workspace to zero, leaving the input phase.

topic-7-4-1.title: Read the relative sign
topic-7-4-1.caption: The final H makes equal and opposite oracle signs distinguishable. M reads the parity of the two function values, not their individual values.

topic-7-4-3.title: Preparation and readout both matter
topic-7-4-3.caption: With target input 1, the first H prepares the minus state and the full circuit returns the desired parity. Starting the target at 0 instead makes a plus state and always yields zero. Omitting the final H gives random input-wire outcomes.

topic-9-1-1.title: Test a candidate label
topic-9-1-1.caption: A computational-basis input and a blank target implement one predicate test. M reads whether x is marked; this is classical value-query behaviour represented with the reversible oracle.

topic-9-1-2.title: Prepare and mark four candidates
topic-9-1-2.caption: Two H gates prepare the uniform state. Controlled-Z marks 11 by changing only its sign; it does not change immediate measurement probabilities.

topic-9-2-1.title: Group outcomes of the search circuit
topic-9-2-1.caption: The bundled wire carries the n-qubit search register. Good and bad components group its basis labels; they are not separate physical qubits.

topic-9-2-2.title: Readout before amplification
topic-9-2-2.caption: Measuring the uniform preparation succeeds with probability M/N. The angle in the text describes this circuit’s initial amplitudes, not a second register.

topic-9-2-3.title: One pair of reflections
topic-9-2-3.caption: On a bundled register the oracle acts first and D second. Their product rotates the two-component state by 2 theta; D is the reflection about the prepared uniform state.

topic-9-3-1.title: Repeated Grover iterations
topic-9-3-1.caption: The repeated gate denotes k uses of the oracle-and-reflection pair, not one elementary gate. Measure only after these coherent iterations.

topic-9-3-3.title: Verify a measured candidate
topic-9-3-3.caption: After a search run returns candidate x, a separate basis-input query checks it. A failed check calls for another run with the prescribed iteration schedule and budget.

notes: Accept only when the measured predicate bit is 1.
circuits.label: Verification run

topic-9-4-1.title: An arbitrary coherent preparation
topic-9-4-1.caption: A is the full reversible preparation circuit. Its success probability is the total weight on good outputs; the bundled wire includes any required coherent workspace.

topic-9-4-3.title: Pay for both preparation and its inverse
topic-9-4-3.caption: One amplification round applies the success reflection, inverse preparation, zero-state reflection, and preparation. Repeat the round coherently before measuring; the zero-reflection cost must also be included when significant.

topic-8-1-1.title: Wire order and gate order
topic-8-1-1.caption: The two wires identify subsystems. U followed by V on the first wire gives VU; W on the separate wire may run independently.

topic-8-1-2.title: The oracle inside a circuit
topic-8-1-2.caption: Deutsch’s algorithm uses one oracle gate between its preparation and readout gates. The Uf box specifies a joint operation, not its internal gate count.

topic-8-2-1.title: Rotations and phase gates
topic-8-2-1.caption: These are separate single-qubit circuits. Rotation parameters are continuous; S and T are fixed phase operations.

topic-8-3-1.title: Local gates preserve product states
topic-8-3-1.caption: No wire connection appears in this circuit. Each output depends only on the input on its own wire, so local gates cannot create entanglement from a product input.

topic-8-3-2.title: Local gates with entangling connections
topic-8-3-2.caption: A representative circuit uses arbitrary single-qubit gates and CNOT. This finite example shows the gate repertoire; it does not claim that two CNOTs synthesize every two-qubit unitary.

notes: U, V, W, R, S, T here denote arbitrary single-qubit unitaries.

topic-8-3-3.title: Approximate a gate sequence
topic-8-3-3.caption: Each Vj approximates the corresponding Uj with a specified operator-norm error. The diagram compares two circuits; it does not assert an exact finite-alphabet synthesis.

topic-8-4-1.title: Count gates, layers, and wires
topic-8-4-1.caption: Three initial Hadamards run in parallel, followed by two successive CNOTs. This example has five gates, depth three, and width three when these gates are available directly.

topic-8-4-2.title: Route an interaction through a neighbour
topic-8-4-2.caption: For a linear three-qubit layout, SWAP brings the third logical qubit next to the first. CNOT acts there, and the second SWAP restores the original ordering. Each SWAP itself requires implementation.

topic-8-4-3.title: Encoding is not cloning
topic-8-4-3.caption: Two CNOTs encode one unknown qubit into a joint three-qubit state. This is the repetition-code encoding used for bit-flip protection; it is not a complete error-correction or fault-tolerance circuit.

topic-10-1-1.title: Specify the input and success condition
topic-10-1-1.caption: Cn is the complete circuit selected by the input length n. The bundled wire includes input and initialized workspace; the measured output is interpreted according to the stated task.

topic-10-1-2.title: A circuit family and its cost
topic-10-1-2.caption: An abstract Cn box stands for a full circuit whose cost has been counted separately. The growth estimate describes that construction, not a lower bound on every algorithm.

topic-10-1-3.title: Count queries separately from gates
topic-10-1-3.caption: This illustrative schedule uses two queries. U0, U1, U2 and the oracle implementations may each contain many elementary gates; the bundled wire includes workspace.

notes: Oracle uses: 2; total gates and register width require separate accounting.

topic-10-2-1.title: Checking a certificate
topic-10-2-1.caption: The reversible implementation of a classical verifier preserves x and certificate w and writes V(x,w) into a blank bit. This checks a supplied certificate; it does not find one. Internal workspace is suppressed.

notes: Accept if the final bit is 1.

topic-10-2-2.title: A bounded-error decision circuit
topic-10-2-2.caption: A BQP circuit family must be uniformly generated with polynomial gate count and workspace. Each run yields a decision bit; repeated fresh runs can reduce its error.

topic-10-2-3.title: Search in its query model
topic-10-2-3.caption: The search circuit has a proved quadratic query advantage. This does not establish a general computational-class separation or give a factoring construction.

notes: Unique mark: \(k=O(\sqrt N)\) queries for constant success.
Factoring uses a different construction, beyond this book’s derivation.

topic-10-3-1.title: The circuit family covered by a query bound
topic-10-3-1.caption: A query algorithm alternates oracle calls with operations independent of the hidden input. The two-query drawing is one instance of this general form; a lower bound must cover every allowed sequence.

notes: The hidden input enters only through the oracle gates.

topic-10-3-2.title: Compare hidden inputs in the same circuit
topic-10-3-2.caption: The two circuits use identical intervening gates and differ only in the oracle. The lower-bound argument compares their final states; the diagram itself is not a proof of the bound.

notes: Marked oracle: one hidden position changes phase.
Reference oracle: no positions change phase.

topic-10-3-3.title: Queries increase polynomial degree
topic-10-3-3.caption: The two-query example gives amplitudes of degree at most two in the hidden Boolean bits and acceptance probabilities of degree at most four. The text generalizes this to T queries.

topic-10-4-1.title: Coherent operations before readout
topic-10-4-1.caption: The preparation A and its associated reflection must be implemented coherently. The success reflection changes phase; the prepared-state reflection converts that phase change into a change in success probability.

topic-10-4-2.title: A finite circuit still has a sampled output
topic-10-4-2.caption: A computably described finite circuit can be simulated classically, potentially at enormous cost. Its measurement returns a sample, not its complete amplitude list or a general halting decision.

notes: One run returns y; a full classical simulation tracks the joint amplitudes.

topic-10-4-3.title: A starting circuit for error correction
topic-10-4-3.caption: This repetition encoding is a concrete continuation toward error correction. It creates one encoded joint state, not three clones. Syndrome extraction and recovery still need further circuits; period finding is a separate continuation.

appendix-a.title: A stack remembers the unmatched prefix
appendix-a.caption: Reading \(aabb\) pushes for each \(a\) and pops for each \(b\). The empty stack at the end certifies matching counts in this example; checking order is also required.

appendix-b.title: A derivation generates a string
appendix-b.caption: Apply \(S\to aSb\) twice, then \(S\to\) empty string. This demonstrates generation of \(aabb\); it does not yet give a procedure for rejecting arbitrary strings.

appendix-c.title: Use conjugation when normalizing
appendix-c.caption: For the complex vector \((3,4i)\), the squared norm is \(9+16=25\). Dividing by five gives a unit vector; the imaginary coordinate contributes positively to its norm.

appendix-d.title: Different ensembles can yield the same density matrix
appendix-d.caption: An equal mixture of \(\ket0\) and \(\ket1\) and an equal mixture of \(\ket+\) and \(\ket-\) both yield \(I/2\). No measurement on the qubit alone identifies which ensemble was used.

appendix-e.title: Queries can increase polynomial degree
appendix-e.caption: Starting from amplitudes independent of hidden input bits, each Boolean query raises their degree by at most one. Squaring magnitudes gives the factor of two for acceptance probabilities.

topic-3-2-1.title: The product rule along one path
topic-3-2-1.caption: The weight of the path \(i\to j\to k\), with step \(S\) and then step \(T\), is the product of its two arrow weights.

topic-3-2-2.title: Sum the paths to a common endpoint
topic-3-2-2.caption: Each route passes through an intermediate configuration \(j\). Multiply along each route, then sum over all intermediate configurations; the dots stand for any additional routes.

notes.text: \(\bra kTS\ket i=\sum_j\bra kT\ket j\,\bra jS\ket i\)

topic-3-2-3.title: Update one component of the state
topic-3-2-3.caption: Each initial weight \(v_i\) contributes \(\bra jS\ket i\,v_i\) to the new weight at \(j\). The new state contains one such sum for every output configuration.

topic-3-3-1.title: Signs multiply along a path
topic-3-3-1.caption: Each row is a path through configurations \(i\), \(j\), and \(k\), with transition weights on the arrows. One negative arrow gives path weight \(-1/4\); two negative arrows give path weight \(+1/4\). The rows are separate examples.

topic-3-3-2.title: Cancellation at a common endpoint
topic-3-3-2.caption: Two paths to the same configuration \(k\) contribute \(ca\) and \(db\). With \(a=b=c=1/2\) and \(d=-1/2\), the contributions cancel although both paths are present.

topic-3-4-1.title: Magnitude and phase of an amplitude
topic-3-4-1.caption: The amplitude \(z=re^{i\phi}\) is a vector of length \(r\) at angle \(\phi\) in the complex plane. Its real and imaginary components are \(r\cos\phi\) and \(r\sin\phi\); its squared magnitude is \(r^2\).

topic-3-4-2.title: Relative phase changes how paths combine
topic-3-4-2.caption: Prepare equal-magnitude amplitudes with relative phase \(\phi\), then apply \(H\). Only the routes to final configuration zero are shown. The phase changes their sum, even though it leaves the initial probabilities unchanged.

topic-4-2-2.title: Measurement and its conditional state
topic-4-2-2.caption: For \(\ket\psi=(\sqrt3/2)\ket0+(1/2)\ket1\), the first measurement gives the indicated probabilities. Each branch leaves a definite state, so an immediate repeat gives the same result.

notes.text: Arrow labels are probabilities; nodes are conditional states.

topic-3-1-1.title: A state of one bit
topic-3-1-1.caption: Each configuration carries a weight. The state is the pair of weights \(v_0\) and \(v_1\).

topic-3-1-3.title: RESET merges two configurations
topic-3-1-3.caption: RESET sends both configurations to \(0\). A run that reaches \(0\) does not record where it started, so RESET is deterministic but not reversible.

topic-5-1-1.title: Input, unitary evolution, and readout
topic-5-1-1.caption: The wire carries the quantum input through the complete unitary Uf to measurement. M produces one classical result; Uf may contain many elementary gates.

topic-5-1-2.title: Gates compose in time order
topic-5-1-2.caption: The same wire passes through U1 and then U2. The output is U2 U1 applied to the input.

topic-5-1-3.title: One run gives one result
topic-5-1-3.caption: Each fresh run prepares its input and repeats the circuit. The double line carries the sampled classical result, not the state’s amplitude list.

topic-5-2-3.title: Phase becomes an output probability
topic-5-2-3.caption: The final Hadamard converts the relative phase into measurement probabilities.

topic-5-3-1.title: The Pauli gates on one wire
topic-5-3-1.caption: These are four separate circuits on the same arbitrary input. The displayed output vectors include their phase factors.

topic-5-3-2.title: A matrix sum is not a gate sequence
topic-5-3-2.caption: H equals the normalized matrix sum of X and Z. Applying X then Z instead gives their product ZX, a different circuit.

topic-6-1-2.title: A superposition without entanglement
topic-6-1-2.caption: H acts only on the first wire; the second remains zero. The output is a product despite having two nonzero joint amplitudes.

topic-9-3-2.title: Choose how many iterations to apply
topic-9-3-2.caption: The circuit repeats the oracle-and-reflection pair k times before measurement. More iterations can decrease success; the interactive readout below tracks this same circuit.

topic-6-5-1.title: Evaluate f on every input
topic-6-5-1.caption: Two H gates spread the inputs over all four strings. One application of \(U_f\) then places each input beside its own value: \(\tfrac12\sum_x\ket x\ket{f(x)}\).

topic-6-5-2.title: Measure a parallel evaluation
topic-6-5-2.caption: Measuring all three wires after the parallel evaluation returns one input \(x\), chosen at random, with its value \(f(x)\). The other pairs are not available from the same run.

topic-6-5-3.title: Interfere the input branches
topic-6-5-3.caption: After \(U_f\), H on each input combines contributions from all four inputs. A constant \(f\) returns the readout 00 with certainty; for AND the target’s record keeps the branches apart, and 00 has probability \(5/8\).

topic-4-1-2.title: Paths from an initial state to a final state
topic-4-1-2.caption: The arrow into configuration \(j\) carries \(\braket j\psi\), and the arrow from \(j\) into the final state carries \(\braket\phi j\). Each path multiplies the two and the paths add, giving \(\braket\phi\psi\). For the final state \(\ket0\), only the path through \(0\) contributes, because \(\braket00=1\) and \(\braket01=0\).
